background.definition: Fragile X syndrome is a mutation of the FMR-1 gene located on chromosome X-q27.3 that codes for the fragile X mental retardation protein (FMRP) which is needed for normal brain development. Lack of this protein results in fragile X syndrome, the most common inherited form of mental retardation. A premutation refers to an excess number of repeats in a gene that is at risk of increasing in length during reproduction.

list.listitem: Estimated frequency is approximately 1/4,000 males and 1/8,000 females.

Based on a systematic review and meta-analysis, the prevalence of female carriers of the premutation in the normal population was 34.4 (95% CI: 8.9-60.3) per 10,000; 1:855 for males and 1:291 for females. Full mutation frequency was 1.4 (95% CI: 0.1-3.1) per 10,000 males and 0.9 (95% CI: 0.0-2.9) per 10,000 females in the total population.
This is somewhat lower than an earlier population-based study that reported the frequency of fragile X premutations as 1:468 for males and 1:151 for females.

In a more recent newborn screening study in North Carolina, with over 17,000 infants screened, premutation prevalence rate was 1 per 430 males and 1 per 209 females; only 1 male carrying the full mutation was identified.
Fragile X is the most commonly inherited form of mental retardation.

Women carriers of fragile X premutation alleles appear to have a higher risk of immune-mediated disorders (e.g., autoimmune thyroid disorder, Raynaud's phenomenon, rheumatoid arthritis, Sjögren syndrome).
Sleep apnea may be more common in individuals with fragile X-associated tremors/ataxia syndrome (FXTAS).
Genetic/inherited.

Mutation of FMR-1 the gene on the long arm of the X-q27.3 chromosome resulting in a dynamic triple repeat sequence mutation (CGG). A premutation form exists that leads to two distinct disorders: FXTAS occurring after the fifth decade and premature ovarian failure with onset before age 40 years.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 13 studies, including 2047 cases and 6912 controls, found that compared with controls, FMR1 gene premutation was significantly associated with overt primary ovarian insufficiency, with an OR of 8.13 (95% CI: 4.35-15.19).
The full mutation is defined as over 200 CGG repeats; a normal FMR1 gene has 5-44 CGG repeats and those with the premutation carry an intermediate number of repeats.
Fragile X follows X-linked inheritance, where women carriers transmit the syndrome to 50% of their children. Its actual transmission is dependent on premutations for coding of the FMRP.
Male carriers of the mutation transmit the syndrome to all of their daughters and none of their sons.

In a study of structural brain volumes using MRI across two time points (2-3 years and 4-5 years), the 53 boys with fragile X had generalized brain overgrowth compared to 50 controls and different patterns of brain growth compared to 68 children with ASD.

In another imaging study, abnormalities in the genu and middle cerebellar peduncles were identified using magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS) and diffusion tensor imaging which may play a role in the cognitive impairment and ataxia associated with the FMR1 premutation.

Genetic testing is recommended for any individuals with mental retardation, autism, developmental delays, or a known family member with fragile X syndrome; also consider if ataxia or intention tremor occurs in individuals >50 years old or fertility problems occur in individuals <40 years old. Clinical trials are lacking. C

Diagnostic yield, however, may be low. In one retrospective case series of 507 children with ASD seen in a regional referral center, abnormalities were found on karyotype in 2.3% and in DNA for fragile X in 0.04%.

Newborn screening is feasible. In the screening study mentioned above in North Carolina, 62% of over 18,000 parents approached agreed to screening. Of those refusing screening, major reasons included not wanting to worry about their child, issues with testing very young children, preferring to wait until symptoms appeared, or that the timing of consent made it difficult for them to decide.

Obtain family, medical and psychosocial histories following genetic counseling practice recommendations. C Amniocentesis and CVS are widely used for prenatal diagnosis; amniocentesis is accurate and reliable and may be needed if the placental CVS sample is indeterminate. C

In postnatal diagnosis, amplification by simple PCR on modified DNA is useful for the molecular diagnosis of the fragile X syndrome. However, the gold standard for diagnosis is the southern blot analysis. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Mental retardation, hand flapping, social interaction impairment
Mental Retardation, congenital heart diseases, epicanthal folds, flattened nasal bridge, low set ears, fifth finger clinodactyly, simian crease
Can look like autism, but language is in tact, higher functioning than autism
Both of these syndromes are chromosomal disorders, resulting in mental retardation with varying dysmorphic features

list.listitem: A comprehensive exam is warranted in any child with an intellectual disability to find the etiology. Treatment, prognosis and genetic risk, along with improved health and functional outcomes, are improved with a specific etiology. A comprehensive exam includes medical and developmental history, family history for three generations, dysmorphologic exam, and neuroimaging.
In one study, after the initial diagnosis of a proband with Fragile X, at least 5 additional family members, on average, were diagnosed with an FMR1 mutation.
Obtain family, medical, and psychosocial histories following genetic counseling practice recommendations.

There appears to be a significant time lag between initial presentation and diagnosis. In one study of interviews conducted with 89 families with children with fragile X syndrome, mean age at presentation was 12.3 months in males and 23 months in females while definitive diagnosis was made at a mean of 4 and 9 years, respectively.

Fragile X has many distinguishing physical and clinical features. Dysmorphic features include macrocephaly, large ears, long face, broad forehead, prominent jaw, strabismus, hypotonia, and macro-orchidism. Rates of obesity are also higher among boys with fragile X (31% vs. 18% of same-aged peers).
Neurologic features include late onset progressive tremor, ataxia, dementia, and memory loss. Epilepsy occurs in about 10% to 20% of boys and 6% of girls.
Gynecological features may include fertility problems with premature ovarian failure.
Cognitive deficits include mental retardation (IQ around 40 in males and more variable in females) and language delay.

Areas of strength for boys include receptive vocabulary, visual memory, simultaneous processing, experiential learning, and imitation. Cognitive deficits are relatively stable in boys with fragile X compared to boys with ASD.
Girls with fragile X have similar deficits and strengths as boys but are often less severely affected.

Behavioral problems can be mild or severe and occur in more than 50% of affected patients; these include attention deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), learning disabilities, and hand flapping. Social and repetitive behaviors may be helpful in distinguishing ASD in boys with fragile X who can then be referred for formal testing.

Based on a meta-analysis, children with fragile X syndrome have high prevalence rates of scores above clinical threshold on the Child Behavior Checklist (a tool for measuring psychiatric symptoms; prevalence range 44%-90%), high rates of anxiety (52% and 82%), and, in one study, 29% were diagnosed with oppositional defiant disorder.
Many children with fragile X have difficulty with sleep.
The most common neurobehavioral manifestation is ASD, which is present in 67% of boys with fragile X. ADHD is present in 73% of boys with fragile X.

In a national data-base study from specialty clinics affiliated with the Fragile X Clinic and Research Consortium, 51% of 427 male and 18% of 120 female children were diagnosed with ASD based on clinician assessment using Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition criteria. Children diagnosed with ASD also had higher rates of epilepsy (20.7% vs. 7.6% without ASD) and behavioral problems.

Fragile X is characterized by a triple repeat sequence mutation CGG in the x-linked gene coding for fragile X mental retardation protein. If the protein is freely expanded, fragile X syndrome results.
FMRP-based screening using platelets was shown in one study to be highly discriminatory for fragile X with an area under the ROC curve of 0.948.
Amniocentesis and CVS are widely used for prenatal diagnosis; amniocentesis is accurate and reliable and may be needed if the placental CVS sample is indeterminate.

In postnatal diagnosis, amplification by simple PCR on modified DNA is useful for the molecular diagnosis of the fragile X syndrome. However, the gold standard for diagnosis is the southern blot analysis.
In a study of 49 individuals with fragile X syndrome, the Pediatric Anxiety Rating Scale-Revised (PARS-R) was feasible, reproducible, and clinical valid for measuring and monitoring anxiety.
MRI shows large caudate nucleus with a small posterior cerebellar vermis. Functional MRI can be useful for evaluating patients with FXTAS.

Screen persons of either sex who have mental retardation, ASD, or developmental delay or physical stigmata of fragile X, as well as individuals with a family history of mental retardation for fragile X.

Order Southern blot analysis to assess the number of trinucleotide repeats CGG to assess for premutation or full mutation. If the analysis shows premutation, monitor for premature ovarian failure and FXTAS. If the analysis shows full mutation, monitor for mental retardation and ASD.
Patients with premutation and full mutation can benefit from genetic counseling for manifestations and future risks, and educational interventions.
Stimulant medications are well established treatments for ADHD; however, if ADHD is associated with Fragile X, stimulant medication may cause mood instability. B
Educational interactions and therapies are the primary mode of treatment along with occupational and speech therapy. C

Folic acid therapy and L-Leucovorin 15mg/day are often recommended. A meta-analysis identified 10 studies and found no overall benefit. However, no major side effects were noted. A Cochrane review found insufficient data to determine the effect of folic acid in individuals with fragile X.

L-acetylcarnitine, the acetylated form of carnitine that is abundant in cerebral tissue, was found in one meta-analysis of two studies to have a net benefit. However, authors of a Cochrane review of two low-quality RCTs concluded that there was no clear evidence of benefit on intellectual functioning or hyperactive behavior.

Memantine, an uncompetitive N-methyl-d-aspartate receptor antagonist currently approved for treatment of moderate to severe Alzheimer's disease, was not effective for tremor or behavior in patients with FXTAS.

Donepezil therapy over 12 weeks was also not effective on intelligence or behavior in an RCT of 20 boys with fragile X syndrome. However, in an RCT with 42 patients with fragile X syndrome, there were no significant differences between donepezil and placebo groups in cognitive or behavioral (total score or subscales of the aberrant behavior checklist) outcomes.

Acamprosate, of unknown mechanism of action and used to reduce cravings in alcohol dependence, was associated with a significant improvement in social behavior and a reduction in inattention/hyperactivity in an open-label trial of 12 young adults with fragile X syndrome. Additional testing is needed.
In a phase 2 trial 24-week trial of adult males with fragile X syndrome, use of a phosphodiesterase-4D allosteric inhibitor improved cognitive performance in domains related to language.
Other options include clonidine, guanfacine, and valproic acid, but data are limited. Similarly, a few studies evaluating lovastatin and acamprosate have been completed but there are few RCTs.

ADHD: Methylphenidate is a well established stimulant for the treatment of ADHD. While it may improve irritability, anxiety, moodiness, and hyperactivity, there is an increase in motor tics, social isolation, and mood instability with outbursts.

In an RCT of 66 children with fragile X syndrome, minocycline treatment for 3 months resulted in greater global improvement and improvement in mood-related behaviors than placebo, with no difference in side effects. A previous small uncontrolled trial suggested benefit in language and behavior with minocycline.
Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors have been effective in reducing anxiety but there are no RCTs.
Aggression: Antipsychotics such as risperidone and aripiprazole may be effective.

Citicoline is a natural compound that activates the biosynthesis of structural phospholipids in neuronal membranes and increases noradrenaline and dopamine levels in the central nervous system. In an open-label pilot study of citicoline in 10 patients with FXTAS, there was some improvement in anxiety over 12 months.
A small crossover trial with 18 patients, 12 of whom completed the study, suggests that melatonin may modestly improve sleep duration and latency.

In an open label, phase 1/2 trial of transdermal Cannabidiol administered twice daily for 12 weeks in 20 children and adolescents, there was a clinically meaningful reduction in anxiety and behavioral symptoms based on the Anxiety, Depression, and Mood Scale. Most (85%) reported treatment-emergent adverse events of which 70% were mild in severity, and no serious adverse events were reported.
Depending on the degree of mental retardation, educational intervention therapy, including computerized tools, may be the main approach to maximizing intellectual outcomes, as well as social support.

In an RCT of Cogmed, a computer/tablet-based working memory training program, parent- and teacher-reported attention and distractibility significantly improved across both the adaptive (difficulty level adjusted to performance) and nonadaptive treatment arms with no differences between groups; many changes were maintained at 3-month follow-up.

A parent-implemented language intervention delivered by a language-speech pathologist over teleconferencing was helpful in improving language in a small 12-week RCT; there was no difference between placebo and lovastatin arms.

Use a family network for case identification with prompt follow-up by medical personel such as a genetic counselor. In a qualitative study of African American mothers of children with fragile X, concerns were expressed about delayed testing once concerns were expressed, insensitive delivery of the diagnosis with outdated information provided, and problems with communicating with family members.

Reproductive alternatives are discussed including adoption, egg donation, foster care, or raising an affected child. The presence of AGG interruptions appears to reduce the risk of transmission of a full mutation for women with premutation alleles considering pregnancy.

Psychiatrists may be consulted to assist in controlling behavior, such as temper tantrums, self injurious behavior, screaming, head banging, using a behavior modification technique. Authors of a systematic review found behavioral approaches promising.
Speech therapy is indicated if there is speech delay.
Detailed health supervision and management guidelines are available from the AAP.

Medical problems associated with Fragile X based on a database of 260 children and adults seen at 9 U.S. Fragile X specialty clinics included the following: Recurrent otitis media (52.6% [46.4–58.8%] vs. 12.6% in the general population) Strabismus (16.4% [11.9–20.9%] vs. 2.6-4%) Seizures (10.0% [6.4–13.7%] vs. 1.2%) Obstructive sleep apnea (7.2% [3.9–10.5%] vs. 1.2%)

Patients with fragile X syndrome can have a normal life expectancy. Comorbid conditions and behaviors influence this, such as the degree of mental retardation, degree of behavioral problems and the degree of self injurious behavior. C

Authors of a literature review found that adults with fragile X tended to be independent in activities of daily living such as bathing and feeding and, while 70% of adult males and 50% of adult females lived at home, many were working full time (48% of females and 20% of males).

Using data from a national family survey, adult independence was influenced by co-occurring mental conditions (autism spectrum disorders for men and affect problems for women), functional skills (men), and ability to interact appropriately (women). B
With premutation, watch for intention tremor, gait ataxia and dementia after age 50 years in men. B

Acquisition of adaptive behavior (eg, daily living skills like meal preparation) was found to slow as children with fragile X syndrome age, based on a longitudinal study of 275 children and adolescents with fragile X syndrome and 225 typically-developing children and adolescents.
In females <40 years, monitor for increased levels of FSH and premature ovarian failure. B

Low quality of life and high stress were common concerns among family members, but the degree of child behavior problems accounted for the varying degrees of stress, depression, anxiety, and anger within the family. C
Prognosis for a stable home environment is decreased with comorbid autism or ADHD. C
In men over age 50 years with ataxia and intention tremor or women over 40 years with premature ovarian failure, consider fragile X premutations.
Reproductive counseling is recommended for female carriers of the fragile X gene and affected males.
